articleHeadlineTranslated: Is pneumonia in children contagious?
articleHeadline: Viêm phổi ở trẻ có lây?
articleSummary: Contagiousness of pediatric pneumonia depends on cause: viral or bacterial pneumonia spreads via respiratory droplets; pneumonia from aspiration or chemicals is not contagious. Common pathogens include viruses such as RSV, influenza, parainfluenza, metapneumovirus, and adenovirus; and bacteria such as Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis, and Mycoplasma pneumoniae. Transmission occurs via droplets and indirect contact with hands, toys, and surfaces. Contagion window varies: bacterial pneumonia often becomes less contagious after 24–48 hours of appropriate antibiotics and fever resolution; viral pneumonia remains contagious during acute symptoms. No fixed isolation period. Return to school after fever-free for at least 24 hours without antipyretics and the child is well. Prevention includes handwashing, coughing hygiene, masks in public, not sharing utensils, cleaning surfaces, ventilation; vaccination against influenza, pneumococcus, Hib. Seek care for high fever or worsening breathing. Do not self-prescribe antibiotics. BS.CKII Bùi Thị Khuyên, Pediatrics, Tam Anh Clinic Cau Giay, Hanoi.

articleHeadline: Severe Hand, Foot and Mouth Disease Outbreak in Vietnam Traced to a Single
articleSummary: Severe hand, foot and mouth disease (HFMD) outbreak in Vietnam in 2023 was traced to a single introduction of enterovirus A71 subgenogroup B5, a lineage first detected in the region around November 2022. Enterovirus A71 can cause brainstem encephalitis, acute flaccid paralysis, pulmonary edema and cardiogenic shock; typical HFMD symptoms include fever, mouth ulcers and a rash on hands, feet and buttocks. Lab tests found no substantial antigenic drift between 2014 and 2023 B5 viruses, arguing against immune evasion. Serology revealed profound susceptibility among young children: only 6.7% of 0–<3-year-olds had neutralizing antibodies one month before the outbreak, with similarly low levels six months prior. As antibodies rose during the epidemic, infections declined, underscoring serosurveillance as an early warning tool and outbreak-control aid.

articleHeadline: Woman's Hallucinations And Headaches Hid A Terrifying Diagnosis: Doctors Discovered A Parasite In Her Brain
articleSummary: In the Philippines, a 52-year-old woman with four months of headaches and visual hallucinations, plus speech difficulties, was diagnosed with neurocysticercosis. MRI showed multiple brain cysts, some containing a bright spot—the scolex of Taenia solium larva. EEG revealed abnormal activity suggesting seizures. She received antiparasitic therapy and seizure treatment; within a month her symptoms resolved and follow-up scans showed cysts shrinking and the bright scolex spots disappearing. Neurocysticercosis arises when T. solium eggs are ingested, traveling to the brain via the bloodstream after fecal contamination of food, water, or surfaces. Eggs can cause disease without pork consumption; possible exposure in evacuation centers with poor sanitation over the prior year. Symptoms may emerge months to years after infection and include headaches, seizures, confusion, or language difficulties. Prevention emphasizes hygiene, safe water and food, and treating intestinal tapeworms.

articleHeadline: In Brazil's Leprosy Heartland, a Hidden Web of Neglected Infections
articleSummary: In Governador Valadares and surrounding communities in the Doce River valley, Minas Gerais, Brazil, a 2026 study tested 1,311 residents aged 3+ for immune signatures of Hansen's disease and two intestinal parasites using a multiplexed bead assay. Hansen's disease exposure/history: 5.5% reported prior disease; 7.2% were anti-LID-1 positive, indicating exposure to Mycobacterium leprae. Parasitic infections were common: 63.8% reported at least one past parasitic disease; serology showed 11.7% SEA antibodies for Schistosoma mansoni and 5.3% NIE antibodies for Strongyloides stercoralis. Rural residence was associated with higher odds of anti-LID-1 positivity (aOR 1.79, 95% CI 1.07–3.38) and Hansen's disease history (aOR 1.97, 95% CI 1.14–3.38). Immunological cross-associations were suggestive but not statistically significant. The findings reveal simultaneous, overlapping exposure to leprosy and helminths, underscoring subclinical transmission and guiding surveillance despite M. leprae culture challenges.

articleSummary: On Oct 2, at Russia’s Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute, a 28-year-old female researcher died of unexplained pneumonia amid rumors she shattered plague tubes. About 5,000 samples were tested with no dangerous pathogens detected; roughly 200 contacts were under medical observation with no abnormalities. The WHO assessed local plague risk as medium-low; Russia-wide risk is low. Plague is caused by Yersinia pestis, a Class A infectious disease in China. Transmission occurs via flea bites, contact with infected or dead rodents (rats or jerboas), and pneumonic spread by droplets. Incubation is 1–6 days; symptoms include fever above 39°C, painful inguinal or axillary lymphadenopathy, hemoptysis, and dyspnea; untreated mortality is high. Modern medicine can control it: isolate suspected cases and start antibiotics (streptomycin, gentamicin, doxycycline, ciprofloxacin) promptly; close contacts may receive prophylaxis. Prevention emphasizes avoiding wildlife handling, outdoor protective clothing, anti-flea measures, reporting symptoms, and following 'Three Nos, Three Reports'; urban risk remains low.

articleSummary: Leishmania braziliensis-driven cutaneous leishmaniasis in Brazil and other regions of the Americas is targeted by covalent inhibitors of its dihydroorotate dehydrogenase (DHODH). Researchers from USP's FCFRP developed the first covalent DHODH inhibitors, derived from barbituric acid, that form a covalent bond with cysteine 131 in the parasite enzyme. Among tested compounds, designated 2i showed strong inhibition of L. braziliensis DHODH activity, efficacy against parasite forms cultured in the lab, and crucially no inhibition of the human DHODH nor toxicity to tested immune cells. X-ray crystallography confirmed active-site occupancy and covalent linkage, guiding further optimization for potency and selectivity. Next steps include human-cell toxicity assessment, testing against other Leishmania species, and animal-model studies, ahead of any clinical trials. This work supports a potential new approach for an NTD that still relies on older, toxic therapies.
